name: Donkey (South Indian)
description: Donkey (known as 'Kazhuda' in Tamil/Malayalam or 'Gaadida' in Telugu) is a popular shedding card game played in South India. Unlike many Western card games where winning a trick is desirable, in Donkey, the goal is simply to get rid of your cards. Failing to follow suit results in the 'Donkey' penalty: taking all the cards from the current trick into your hand.

history.origins: Donkey is a localized variant of the international family of 'Get Away' or 'Spoons' games. It has been a staple in Indian households for generations, specifically across Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, and Karnataka.
timeline: 20th Century: Becomes a standard family game across the Indian subcontinent.
Modern Era: Often played by children and students during festivities or social gatherings.
history.cultural: In South India, the game is highndenergy and vocal, with players shouting 'Kazhuda!' (Donkey) as soon as someone is forced to pick up cards.
history.evolution: The game evolved to emphasize the 'shame' of being the last player (the Donkey), often involving lighthearted penalties or nicknames for the loser.

setup.dealing: All cards are dealt out as equally as possible. Some players may have one card more than others.

rules.objective: Get rid of all your cards. The last player remaining with cards is the 'Donkey'.
rules.gameplay:
1. Starting: The player holding the Ace of Spades leads the first trick.
2. Following Suit: Every player must follow the suit led.
3. Winning a Trick: The highest card of the suit led wins the trick. The winner leads the next trick.
4. The Penalty: If a player cannot follow suit, the trick ends immediately. That player must pick up all cards currently on the table and add them to their hand. That player then leads the next trick.
keyRules: Cards rank: A (high), K, Q, J, 10... 2 (low).
A player is 'Safe' once they have no cards left.
If you lead a card and everyone follows suit, the cards in the trick are discarded and removed from the game.

strategy.basic: Get rid of your high cards (A, K, Q) as early as possible in suits where you have many cards.
strategy.intermediate: If you are forced to lead a trick, lead a suit where you have only one or two cards (a 'short' suit) to increase your chance of being unable to follow suit later (which lets you dump other high cards).
strategy.advanced: Trap Tactics: If you know an opponent has no cards left in a particular suit, lead that suit to force them to take a penalty if they are the one supposed to follow suit.

If you have the Ace and King of a suit, lead the Ace first to clear it out.
